item.content:encoded:
You reread a text 14 times to try and understand the tone the other person used. They didn’t text “good morning” like they usually do, and now you’re wondering if you said something wrong. Your partner was unusually quiet during dinner, and you’re already preparing yourself for the “we need to talk” conversation. Sound familiar? These are all signs of an anxious attachment style.
The frustrating part is that even when everything in your relationship is going fine, it’s hard to stop worrying that something’s wrong. You might find yourself feeling insecure, needing extra reassurance, or assuming the worst over something small. Sometimes, those anxious attachment triggers can make a completely normal situation feel like a MUCH bigger problem.
Recognizing these patterns isn’t about diagnosing yourself. It’s about understanding why certain situations bother you so much and figuring out how to handle those feelings when they come up.
We’ve rounded up a few Dear Media episodes where hosts and guests talk about anxious attachment, what it looks like in relationships, and how to start working through it. We’re sharing some of their most helpful advice below, without all the complicated psychology terms.
What Is Anxious Attachment and How It Affects Your Relationships
If you’ve ever spent an entire afternoon worrying about a text that went unanswered, you probably know how exhausting that can be. And when it happens regularly, even little things like a change in someone’s tone or a bit of emotional distance can leave you questioning where you stand.
Learning about anxious attachment styles can help you understand why you react this way, especially if you have a strong fear of rejection or find yourself constantly looking for reassurance. It can also help you recognize which habits might be making navigating relationships harder than it needs to be.
On Girls Gotta Eat, neuroscientist Andrew Huberman explained that attachment styles are way older and go much deeper than dating. As an infant you come into the world helpless, and attachments are how we first learn whether or not our anxiety can be soothed.
Those brain areas and chemicals used in infant attachment don’t magically change. They’re the same ones we use in adulthood for romantic attachment. In other words, your reactions are literally how you were wired.
A quick but important note:
What Is Anxious Attachment Style?
An anxious attachment style is a pattern in relationships where you want to feel close to someone else, but you’re worried that they’ll lose interest or eventually leave. And we’re not talking about occasionally feeling insecure in your relationship. Almost everyone experiences that from time to time.
The difference is how often those worries come up and how much they affect you. Maybe you need your partner to reassure you that everything’s okay, even when they haven’t given you a reason to think otherwise. Or you start overthinking every little interaction because you’re worried something has changed. When that becomes a regular part of your relationships, it could be a sign of anxious attachment.
On Girls Gotta Eat, Huberman described how researchers first learned about attachment styles in babies using the “strange situation” setup. This is where a caregiver leaves the room and comes back.
The interesting part is not how the child reacts when the caregiver leaves, but how they react when the caregiver comes back. Anxiously attached babies get agitated. They don’t even feel fully better when the caregiver does come back. Take this situation and swap it: you’re the baby and your partner’s the caregiver. (Weird, we know. Stick with us here.) But basically, it’s the SAME situation.
Attachment styles shape how people respond to emotional closeness, to perceived rejection, and to uncertainty in general. On Girls Gotta Eat, Dr. Amir Levine described attachment as a surveillance system. It’s almost like there’s a thread between you and the person you’re attached to. When they’re “there,” you can tug the thread and feel they’re holding onto it. But when they leave and the thread snaps, it’s unsettling.
Signs of Anxious Attachment Style
Common signs of anxious attachment style include:
- Having a strong fear of rejection or abandonment, even when a partner hasn’t given you a reason to worry
- Needing your partner to regularly reassure you that everything is okay
- Seeking constant connection and getting anxious when someone takes too long to respond
- Overthinking little things, like a shorter text than usual or canceled plans
- Having a hard time calming yourself down without reassurance from your partner
- Sending multiple texts, starting arguments, or pulling away to see if your partner will react
- Struggling to focus on other things when you’re worried about where you stand in your relationship
When you basically have ALL of these warning signs going off at once, it’s exhausting. It’s also confusing. But this isn’t a “you’re stuck this way forever” kind of thing. You can intentionally work on the type of attachment you have in relationships.
How Anxious Attachment Style Affects Relationships
Emotional Triggers Hijack Your Day
With an anxious attachment style, your nervous system pretty much treats small disruptions like total emergencies. You could’ve had the most amazing weekend with your partner and everything could’ve gone perfectly as planned. But come Monday morning, they forget to text you when they wake up. For an anxious person? That signals the beginning of the end.
The anxious person is SO sensitive to potential danger in a relationship that they feel relationships can be very fragile. A forgotten text can’t just be an accident; it HAS to mean something. In short, anxious attachment triggers don’t wait for actual evidence to sound the nervous system alarms.
Seeking Constant Reassurance Can Push Partners Away
If you’re the type of person who looks for constant contact and reassurance, it can unintentionally create the exact emotional distance you’re afraid of.
On The Bossticks, Harvard-trained Behavioral Scientist Logan Ury actually broke down a super common pattern: Anxious and avoidant attachments mixed together. When an anxious partner pairs with an avoidant one, you get the anxious-avoidant loop. One chases while one pulls away, reinforcing each other’s triggers. The anxious person’s story is “I’m going to chase you and you’re going to pull away,” and the avoidant person’s story is “you’re going to smother me.”
Ironically though, Ury says that people get addicted to this cycle of not knowing. She compared it to a slot machine, which is exactly how people start to confuse anxiety for chemistry.
You Confuse Intensity With Connection
If you have an anxious ambivalent attachment style, you might find yourself drawn to someone who’s hot and cold because you never really know where you stand with them. Remember the slot machine example we mentioned earlier? Ury brought up research from psychologist B.F. Skinner to explain why that unpredictability can make it so hard to stop seeking someone’s attention. Partial reward schedules get us hooked to inconsistent people.
People should be with someone consistent and securely attached who shows up, but they think that is boring and get drawn to the person where they do not know when they will get attention.
It Can Make You Lose Yourself
When you’re constantly worried about keeping your partner happy or making sure they won’t leave, it’s easy to start putting your own needs aside. You might find yourself changing your plans, avoiding certain conversations, or agreeing to things you don’t actually want to do.
But having an insecure attachment doesn’t mean you’ll always feel this way. On Girls Gotta Eat, Huberman explained that attachment patterns can change over time, and the person you’re in a relationship with can make a difference, too.
If some of these behaviors sound familiar, our guide to unhealthy relationship signs can help you recognize other patterns worth paying attention to.
How to Heal Anxious Attachment Style
When we say “healing an anxious attachment style,” we’re not saying it’s a guaranteed cure. Instead, it’s about building healthier ways to respond to insecurity, uncertainty, and relationship stress. None of this is “fix yourself in a weekend.” It is a practice. Here is where the experts actually agree.
Learn to Self-Soothe
Across each conversation we’ve included with experts, they tend to agree that self-soothing is essential. If you can calm yourself down, you’re essentially not giving someone else control over your entire nervous system.
Huberman explained this perfectly in Girls Gotta Eat. He used tools like getting your sleep right and using breathing to relax as examples. When you feel overwhelmed, these tools basically help you figure out if you’re the problem, or if it’s actually your partner.
When a wave of anxious attachment triggers hits, a few slow breaths before you fire off a reaction genuinely helps.
Get Clear, and Ask for Consistency
Levine’s whole approach is asking for consistency instead of playing games. He told the story of a woman who, after a second date, simply told the guy that it mattered to her that people in her life be consistent, available, and responsive, and that if he could not do that, it would not work.
He said when she put it that way, it did not feel like such a huge ask, and years later they were married with kids.
The magic word, he stressed repeatedly, is not frequency, it is consistency. This is also where setting boundaries is HUGE. You have to learn to stand up for yourself, because there really is a difference between boundaries and attachment styles.
Our guide to how to set boundaries in a relationship without being controlling walks you through this step by step.
Build a Secure Support System
You don’t need ALL of your needs met by one single person. Each expert in the episodes above brings up how important it is to surround yourself with steady, reliable people. This way, when you are seeking support, you have a whole village instead of just one person.
When your sense of safety comes from multiple secure connections, chances are you won’t spiral over one person’s slow reply. That sense of community ultimately comes down to protecting your own nervous system.
Consider Couples Therapy or a Secure Partner
A secure attachment style can seriously be contagious. Levine described how being with his securely attached partner helped him break his own anxious patterns over time.
For couples stuck in the anxious-avoidant loop, couples therapy can be a HUGE help. Both partners eventually learn how to deescalate instead of reinforcing each other’s fears. The goal is a healthier relationship. Emotional closeness feels safe rather than threatening, and emotional distance doesn’t feel like abandonment.
Get Curious Before You React
Instead of treating every uncertain moment as proof that something is going wrong, practice asking what’s actually going on. This slowly teaches you whether your instinct is right or if your internal radar is freaking out for no reason.
It’s also how you build real intimacy! If you want a little inspiration for getting vulnerable, try our list of vulnerable questions to ask your partner.
You’re Not Stuck With an Anxious Attachment Style
TL;DR: Anxious attachment is a consistent fear of being abandoned that turns small moments into big spirals. But it’s a pattern, and you can always change a pattern. When it comes to navigating relationships with an anxious attachment, learn to self-soothe, ask for consistency, and build a secure support system around you.
For more episodes like these, including our roundup of the best podcasts for couples, check out the entire Dear Media network! With over 100 top-rated pop culture, entertainment, and lifestyle podcasts hosted by today’s most talked-about creators, there’s so much you have to catch up on.

item.content:encoded:
Secure Attachment and Youth Loneliness
The role of secure attachment in preventing loneliness and misuse of social media.

Posted September 14, 2026 Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
Key points
- Secure attachments are essential for cognitive, social, and emotional well-being.
- Secure attachments prevent loneliness in young people by fostering bonding with others and social skills.
- Research shows that secure attachments help prevent social media addiction and digital media misuse.
- Parents can learn skills for establishing secure attachments in early life and throught the life cycle.
All the lonely people/Where do they all come from/All the lonely people/Where do they all belong
Lennon and McCartney
With Gen Z now reporting the highest rates of loneliness of any generation, and parents more concerned than ever about the perils of social media amid recent suits against META, researchers and clinicians are increasingly pointing to something we’ve understood for decades: the power of a secure, trusting bond between a child and the adults who raise them.
In the psychological literature, they appear to be crucial for:
- Effective and accurate cognitive functions
- Emotional flexibility
- Feeling safer and more secure
- Finding meaning in experiences
- Self-regulation and managing one’s own feelings and behaviors
- The capacity for intimacy and healthy interpersonal relationships
- Empathy
- Self-awareness and comfort with one’s identity
- Resilience
That’s a lot, and more than any parent or caregiver could possibly want for our kids, teens, and young adults. Kids with secure attachments tend to handle stress better, bounce back from setbacks, form closer friendships, and know themselves more clearly.
But how does this happen?
We humans are pack animals. We need each other. We need relationships.
As Winnicott so clearly pointed out, development requires both a biological endowment and a facilitating environment. The former is rooted in genetics and physical contributions to our development, and the second, perhaps most important part of our life experience, is rooted in relationships.
Dan Siegel summarized the process well. It is a gradual process, beginning and grounded in the first three years of life. Its components include:
- Collaborative Communication: Parental attunement to the child
- Reflective Dialogue: Creating the sense that subjective experience is important and can be shared. This allows the child to be seen
- Repair: Identification and repair of miscommunications and misunderstandings. This requires that both parent and child are mindful of breaches, and use apology and reparations, to mend fences
- Emotional Communication: Sharing and amplifying the positive and mitigating the negative in the interpersonal world of parent and child
- Developing Coherent Narratives: Helping the child and teen develop an internal autobiographical sense of self, and self-awareness, key for self-reflection and a solid sense of identity
Attachment theory has shaped how we understand social and emotional development, parenting, and our own relational patterns. Yet little research addresses how secure attachment protects against specific, longstanding threats to youth development.
In particular, let’s consider loneliness and misuse of social media.
Secure Attachment and Loneliness
On May 3, 2023, The United States Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy released a new Advisory calling attention to the public health crisis of loneliness, isolation, and lack of connection in our country.
According to the Advisory, social connection is a critical but underappreciated contributor to individual overall health, community safety, and resilience. Yet, around half of all U.S. adults report experiencing loneliness, with some of the highest rates among our young people. In fact, today the Gen Z population reports the highest rates of loneliness.
The Surgeon General noted that it is important to “Invest in your relationship with your child or loved one by recognizing that strong, secure attachments are protective and a good foundation for other healthy relationships.”
The report didn’t specify how to foster these attachments (practical examples follow below.) There have been some studies (though few) on how secure attachment mitigates loneliness.
Consider a teenager who gets left out of a group chat, or shows up to find plans have changed without them. A securely attached teen is more likely to mention it to a parent that night, or reach out to another friend, rather than sitting with it alone and assuming the worst about themselves.
Teenagers’ needs for bonding with others, feeling fulfilled, and trust are grounded in their secure attachment profile. As such, they are more likely to seek help and support when distressed, rather than worrying alone. Their sense of connection to others also helps them build highly developed social skills, mitigating temporary isolation without it developing into chronic loneliness. Their sense of connection becomes a part of their autobiographical narrative, and is an important outcome of secure attachment.
Secure Attachment and Problematic Social Media Use
Parents, caregivers, clinicians, and legislators alike have grown concerned about digital media because of both its habit-forming design, and the way young people can misuse it, for instance, for bullying, excessive texting, or ghosting.
Though research is limited, evidence suggests that secure attachments reduce vulnerability to digital media misuse. One study linked insecure attachment to social media addiction, with social support outside of media use acting as a mediator. Another study found secure attachment associated with less addiction and fewer mental health problems.
Secure attachments can reduce a young person’s need to look to social media for validation, emotional regulation, and relief from negative emotions.
None of this means social media is inherently harmful—for many young people, it’s a genuine source of connection and community. The point is more specific: When a young person already feels secure and connected, they’re less likely to depend on a device to meet needs the device can’t fulfill.
What Can Parents and Caregivers Do
With Siegel’s framework in mind, here are some guidelines for nurturing secure attachment:
- When your child is upset, slow down, get on their level, name their feelings, and match your tone before jumping to solutions.
- Ask an open question about their day, and sit with the whole answer with curiosity, instead of moving straight to advice.
- After a blowup, come back later and name what happened. You might say, “I got too frustrated earlier, and I’m sorry” or something similar. The repair matters more than the rupture.
- Identify and name positive moments aloud in the moment they happen so the good moments register. This could look like, “I love that we laughed about that together,” or “I enjoyed watching that with you.”
- To facilitate narrative building skills, ask your teen to tell you about their day as a story instead of a checklist. For example, try phrases like, “Walk me through your day,” as opposed to “How was school.”
Promoting secure attachments is not easy. For many, Siegel’s skills are complicated by real obstacles: parents’ own insecure attachment histories; adverse childhood experiences; economic pressure; disparities related to race, immigration status, or gender identity; unstable family structure; domestic conflict; or psychiatric or physical disability.
It is imperative to recognize these obstacles and seek support — from family, friends, spiritual leaders, or mental health professionals.
And in the process of getting help, parents and caregivers may not only promote secure attachments with their children but earn secure attachment profiles for themselves.
To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
Also posted in a longer form at the Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds at Massachusetts General Hospital.
References
Siegel, D. J. (1999). The developing mind: Toward a neurobiology of interpersonal experience. Guilford Press.
Office of the Surgeon General (OSG). Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory on the Healing Effects of Social Connection and Community [Internet]. Washington (DC): US Department of Health and Human Services; 2023–. PMID: 37792968.
Office of the Surgeon General (OSG). Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory [Internet]. Washington (DC): US Department of Health and Human Services; 2023. PMID: 37721985.
Eichenberg et al. BMC Psychiatry (2024) 24:278. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-024-05709-z
Winnicott DW. The Maturational Processes and the Facilitating Environment. New York: International Universities Press, 1965.
